interactions.label: Why are nosebleeds in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma characteristically se

params.question: Why are nosebleeds in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma characteristically severe and difficult to control?

answers.text: The tumour secretes heparin-like anticoagulant substances that prevent clotting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: JNA does not secrete anticoagulant substances. The severe bleeding is due to a structural property of the tumour's own blood vessels, not a systemic coagulation defect.

answers.text: The tumour erodes the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While JNA can extend towards the middle cranial fossa, the characteristically severe epistaxis is due to the tumour's own abnormal vessels — not erosion of the internal carotid artery.

answers.text: The tumour's blood vessels lack a muscular wall and cannot vasospasm when torn

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. JNA is built from thin-walled vascular channels that lack a muscular media. Unlike normal vessels, they cannot contract when disrupted, so bleeding does not stop spontaneously.

answers.text: The nasal mucosa overlying the tumour is unusually fragile due to chronic inflammation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The severe epistaxis is not due to mucosal fragility but to the intrinsic structural abnormality of the tumour's vessels — they lack smooth muscle and cannot vasospasm.

overallFeedback.feedback: JNA's blood vessels lack a muscular media. Normal vessels vasospasm when cut to limit bleeding, but JNA's thin-walled channels cannot do this. This structural defect explains both the severe epistaxis and the absolute contraindication to biopsy.

Exactly right. JNA's vessels lack smooth muscle in their walls. When disrupted, they cannot vasospasm, leading to uncontrolled arterial-pressure bleeding. This is also why biopsy is absolutely contraindicated.

interactions.label: Pre-operative embolisation of the feeding vessels is an optional step in JNA man

params.question: Pre-operative embolisation of the feeding vessels is an optional step in JNA management, performed only when the tumour is exceptionally large.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Pre-operative embolisation is not optional. JNA management always follows a mandatory two-step sequence: first, selective embolisation of the internal maxillary artery (24–72 hours before surgery), then surgical excision. Skipping embolisation is dangerous because it typically reduces intraoperative blood loss by more than half.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Pre-operative embolisation is not optional — it is the essential first step in a mandatory two-step sequence. Embolisation of the internal maxillary artery 24–72 hours before surgery reduces intraoperative blood loss by more than half. Skipping it is dangerous regardless of tumour size.

params.question: Ohngren's line divides the maxillary sinus into infrastructure and suprastructure. Why do suprastructure tumours carry a worse prognosis than infrastructure tumours?

answers.text: Suprastructure tumours are always histologically higher-grade than infrastructure tumours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tumour grade is independent of location within the sinus. The prognostic difference is determined by proximity to critical anatomical structures, not histological grade.

answers.text: The suprastructure abuts the orbital floor, pterygoid plates, and skull base, making complete excision far more difficult

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Suprastructure tumours are adjacent to the orbital floor, pterygoid plates, and skull base. These critical structures limit the margin of resection and may necessitate radical procedures such as orbital exenteration.

answers.text: The blood supply of the suprastructure is exclusively from the internal carotid artery, increasing surgical risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The blood supply pattern is not the primary reason for the prognostic difference. The worse prognosis is due to proximity to vital structures — the orbit, pterygoid plates, and skull base — which makes complete surgical excision difficult.

answers.text: Suprastructure tumours always present later because they are further from the nasal cavity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While sinonasal malignancies generally present late, the prognostic significance of Ohngren's line relates to anatomical proximity to critical structures, not to timing of symptom onset.

overallFeedback.feedback: Suprastructure tumours (above Ohngren's line) carry a worse prognosis because they lie adjacent to the orbital floor, pterygoid plates, and skull base. This proximity makes complete surgical excision difficult and may necessitate radical procedures including orbital exenteration.

Well analysed. Ohngren's line runs from the medial canthus to the angle of the mandible. Tumours above it abut the orbital floor, pterygoid plates, and skull base — structures that make complete resection difficult and demand more radical surgery.

params.question: A patient from South India who regularly bathes in stagnant ponds presents with a pedunculated nasal polyp that has a strawberry-like surface studded with white sporangia. Which granulomatous disease is most likely?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lupus vulgaris presents with apple-jelly nodules at the nasal tip and shows caseating granulomas with Ziehl-Neelsen positive acid-fast bacilli on histology — not strawberry polyps with sporangia.

Rhinoscleroma, caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, is identified by its pathognomonic biopsy features — Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies. The strawberry polyp with sporangia and stagnant-water exposure point to a different diagnosis.
GPA is a necrotising vasculitis with systemic involvement of the kidneys and lungs, diagnosed by c-ANCA positivity. It does not produce the classic strawberry polyp with sporangia.

Correct. Rhinosporidiosis presents with a strawberry-surfaced polyp studded with white sporangia. It is endemic in South India and linked to bathing in stagnant ponds and rivers. It has no effective medical therapy — complete surgical excision is the only treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is rhinosporidiosis — endemic in South India and linked to bathing in stagnant water. The strawberry-surfaced polyp studded with white sporangia is its hallmark feature. Unlike other granulomatous diseases, it has no effective medical therapy and requires complete surgical excision.

Correct. The strawberry polyp with white sporangia, South Indian origin, and pond-bathing history are classic for rhinosporidiosis. Remember that no medical therapy exists — complete surgical excision is the only option.

params.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and three episodes of severe epistaxis requiring nasal packing. Examination reveals a fleshy pinkish-red mass in the right nasal cavity. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the paranasal sinuses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In a suspected JNA — adolescent male, unilateral obstruction, severe epistaxis — contrast CT is the first investigation. A brightly enhancing mass with the pathognomonic Holman-Miller sign confirms the diagnosis without the catastrophic bleeding risk of biopsy.

answers.text: Incisional biopsy of the mass under local anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Biopsy is absolutely contraindicated when JNA is suspected. The tumour's vessels lack a muscular wall, and biopsy can trigger life-threatening arterial-pressure haemorrhage from the internal maxillary artery that cannot be controlled in an outpatient setting.

answers.text: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and review in four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This presentation — adolescent male with severe recurrent epistaxis and a visible nasal mass — is classic for JNA. Empirical antibiotics would delay diagnosis and risk another dangerous bleed. Unilateral, progressive nasal symptoms must be investigated, not treated empirically.

answers.text: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Any form of tissue sampling — including FNAC — is contraindicated in suspected JNA. The thin-walled vascular channels bleed uncontrollably when disrupted. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging alone; histology waits for the surgical resection specimen.

overallFeedback.feedback: When an adolescent male presents with unilateral obstruction and severe epistaxis, suspect JNA and order contrast CT first. The Holman-Miller sign is pathognomonic. Biopsy is absolutely contraindicated — JNA vessels lack a muscular wall and bleed catastrophically when disrupted.

Correct. The clinical algorithm is clear: adolescent male with severe epistaxis and a nasal mass → suspect JNA → do not biopsy → order contrast CT → look for the Holman-Miller sign → proceed to MRI, embolisation, and excision.
